prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which opened the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the case in this shortlist where a quantitative theoretical prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, flat bands at a magic angle) was followed by an experimental discovery (Jarillo-Herrero and colleagues, correlated insulators and superconductivity) that nobody could have confidently expected, and it created a whole field of moire quantum materials. The credited trio is a clean theory-plus-experiment split, the central phenomenology has been reproduced by many independent groups and extended to other moire platforms, and the support in the opening ballots is the broadest of any candidate (seven of eight members ranked it, six in the top three). My own opening ranked circuit QED first, but on reflection I weigh the breadth of the committee's judgement and the points below about my own position more heavily than my first-place ordering.
statement.case_against: The microscopic mechanism of the superconductivity and the full phase diagram are unsettled, and device-to-device variation from twist-angle disorder complicates comparison. A prize would therefore rest on the platform and the observation of correlated states, not on a settled explanation. Credit also extends beyond three names (for example the first author of the 2018 experiments, other moire experimental groups, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory), which a three-person limit cannot represent, and the field is only about eight years old and still moving fast, so a few more years of waiting would be defensible.

responses.point: B038 is a prediction matched by nature, with large downstream impact, and the three credited names give a clean theory-plus-experiment configuration, while earlier twisted-graphene theory and experimental first authors raise unresolved allocation questions.
responses.response: I agree on the structure of the argument and have moved toward it: the 2011 continuum-model prediction and the 2018 experiments are both decisive, and the instinct to reward a prediction confirmed by nature is the right one. I would qualify the maturity point. Reproducibility of the phases is secure, but I would not let the citation imply a settled pairing mechanism, so I propose wording that credits the prediction and the discovery of correlated and superconducting states, not an explanation of them. On allocation, I do not think the omitted early-theory names change the case, since the magic-angle prediction is specifically the Bistritzer-MacDonald result.

responses.point: B037 (dynamical mean-field theory) should come first as a mature, independently validated and arguably overdue framework, although the omission of Metzner is a genuine fairness concern and its predictive success for real materials is uneven.
responses.response: I take the maturity argument seriously, since DMFT is certainly more established than moire physics, and I share your worry that credit is spread beyond the supplied names. But I disagree on ranking it first. By your own account the attribution problem (Metzner, whose infinite-dimensional limit made the theory possible, is outside the credited set) is serious, and the support for it is thin, with two of eight members ranking it. DMFT is a method whose value is in what it computes, and the discovery element is weaker than for a new experimentally observed phase of matter. I would keep it as a strong later candidate but not as this year's preferred prize.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B045) pair Katori's magic-wavelength idea with Ye's record accuracy, are confirmed across national laboratories at the 1e-18 level, and are the leading route to redefining the second.
responses.response: This is the candidate I find most compelling after B038, and I list it as my first alternative. The attribution is the cleanest of any two-name case on the shortlist and the maturity is not in doubt. My reservation, which you flag yourself, is novelty relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single-system quantum control, and the question of whether the committee is rewarding a measurement-technology advance or a discovery. I also note that only two of eight members put it in their top three, so it does not yet have the breadth of B038. If the committee wants a precision-measurement prize this year, I would support it over my own field.

responses.point: B045 is conceptually clean and technically decisive, B038 follows closely with a clean theory-plus-experiment configuration, and the quantum key distribution trio of Bennett, Brassard and Ekert is a sound reading of the originators.
responses.response: I agree that B038 and B045 are the two strongest on attribution, and that the QKD originators are a defensible trio, which was also my choice among the QKD names. Where I differ is on how to choose between them. Your top pick is a pure measurement achievement, while B038 has opened a new area of physics; I would give weight to that in a year without an overriding reason to prefer precision metrology. I also note that you ranked circuit QED eighth, and I would like to understand whether that reflects a view on the novelty relative to the 2025 prize or a judgement on the cQED contribution itself.

responses.point: Magic-angle graphene is a clean experimental discovery with a clear theoretical prediction, but sample inhomogeneity and twist-angle disorder complicate comparison, and circuit QED (B026) is a tidy prediction-plus-experiment pairing whose timing is distinct from the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I am grateful for the fair reading of circuit QED, but I now think the 2025 overlap is a heavier problem than I allowed in my opening. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, and a second superconducting-circuit award immediately afterwards needs a clear argument that the content is distinct. I believe it is distinct (strong coupling to a single microwave mode and dispersive readout, not tunnelling and energy quantisation), but the committee will reasonably hesitate. Your point on disorder is correct and I would treat it as a reason for modest citation wording, not a reason against the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the superconducting pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene will be clarified soon enough to affect how a citation is framed.
Whether the committee prefers to wait on the moire field or to reward the 2018 discovery now, and how the 2011 prediction should be weighed against it.
How much the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits should reduce the appetite for circuit QED (B026) or other superconducting-qubit candidates this year.
Whether an overlap between the topological insulator entries (B023 and B040) can be packaged into a single fair configuration if the committee turns to condensed matter instead.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue concerning B026 (circuit QED) and, to a lesser degree, B007: I work in superconducting circuit and waveguide QED, direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers, and have Chalmers colleagues (Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson) and frequent collaborators in this area, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I have therefore reduced the weight of my own first-place ranking of B026. For my preferred candidate B038 and the alternative B045, no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
